title: Dependency Inversion
summary: High-level policy should not depend on low-level details. Both depend on an abstraction the policy owns.

steps.title: Policy welded to detail
body: `OrderService` holds the business **policy**. `SqlDatabase` is a **detail**. Yet the policy depends on the detail: change databases and you edit the business code, and you cannot test placing an order without SQL.
1. High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on **abstractions**.
2. Abstractions should not depend on details. Details depend on abstractions.

steps.prompt: Why can you not unit test `OrderService.Place` as written?
options: It creates its own `SqlDatabase`, so a test cannot substitute a harmless store

steps.title: Inverting the arrow
body: The policy declares what it needs, in its own terms:
interface IOrderStore { void Save(Order o); }   // owned by the business side
class SqlOrderStore : IOrderStore { public void Save(Order o) { /* SQL */ } }
Before: `OrderService → SqlDatabase`. After: `OrderService → IOrderStore ← SqlOrderStore`. The arrow from the detail now points *towards* the policy. That flip is the "inversion".
You met the mechanism, constructor injection, in the C# track. DIP is the reason to use it.

options: The business code that needs it
steps.explain: The interface is shaped by what the policy needs (`Save(Order)`), not by what SQL offers (`ExecuteNonQuery`).

steps.prompt: Does the class depend on an abstraction, or on a concrete detail?
Arrange the composition root: build the detail, hand it to the policy, then use the policy.

steps.title: Invert the dependency
prompt: `Notifier` creates its own `SmtpSender`, so it cannot be tested. Refactor:
- `interface IMessageSender { void Send(string to, string text); }`
- `Notifier` receives an `IMessageSender` through its constructor and uses it; `Notify(string user)` sends `Hi <user>` to `<user>@example.com`
The tests pass a fake sender that records messages.
starter: public void Send(string to, string text) => Console.WriteLine($"SMTP to {to}: {text}");
solution: interface IMessageSender { void Send(string to, string text); }
public void Send(string to, string text) => Console.WriteLine($"SMTP to {to}: {text}");
template: Dojo.Eq("to the right address and text", "ada@example.com|Hi ada", dojoFake.Sent.FirstOrDefault() ?? "");
Dojo.Eq("nothing printed by the real sender", "", Dojo.Capture(() => new Notifier(new DojoFakeSender()).Notify("x")));
public void Send(string to, string text) => Sent.Add(to + "|" + text);
